full_text: communications biology Article A Nature Portfolio journal Article in Press https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-026-10800-0 Functional mapping of IFITM3 resolves its antiviral core and deciphers human influenza susceptibility Check for updates Jian Chen 1 , Shufa Zheng2, Jinjin Qi1, Haibo Wu1, Hangping Yao 1 & Min Zheng 1 Genetic variation in interferon-induced transmembrane protein 3 (IFITM3) contributes to inter- individual differences in influenza outcome, yet a comprehensive functional map of IFITM3 variation remains unavailable. Here we show a high-resolution functional atlas of 2,898 IFITM3 variants across three influenza A strains using deep mutational scanning. Our data reveals a functionally constrained central region, providing functional evidence consistent with a Type II membrane topology and highlighting structural features associated with antiviral activity. Comparison with AlphaMissense reveals systematic limitations in predicting the effects of variants within unstructured N-terminal motifs and lipid-embedded domains. Crucially, computational models fail to recognize variants with enhanced antiviral activity, such as G133Q. By integrating this atlas with ClinVar and gnomAD, we provide a functional readout for rare human alleles that may influence susceptibility to infection. These findings provide a resource for interpreting human variation and establish a framework for studying host-directed antiviral mechanisms. Influenza A virus (IAV) infection exhibits remarkable inter-individual heterogeneity, with clinical outcomesranging from mild self-limiting illness to severe viral pneumonia and death1. Human genetic studies have increasingly revealed that this variability is shaped not only by viral factors but also by host-intrinsic antiviral defenses2–4. Among these, Interferon- induced transmembrane protein 3 (IFITM3) stands as a frontline sentinel. By blocking endosomal membrane fusion, IFITM3 restricts a diverse array of enveloped viruses, including IAV and SARS-CoV-25–9. The best- characterized example is the rs12252-C allele, which has been repeatedly associated with severe influenza and COVID-19 outcomes in multiple human cohorts, although its molecular consequences remain incompletely resolved10–14. Such associations suggest that even subtle perturbations in IFITM3 function can profoundly shift infection trajectories. Despite extensive study, the structural basis of IFITM3-mediated viral restriction remains incompletely understood. Prior studies have identified individual functional elements, including the N-terminal Y20XXΦ motif required for endolysosomal trafficking15, S-palmitoylation sites critical for membrane association16; and lysine residues that regulate protein turnover17. In addition, an amphipathic helix (residues 59–68) has been proposed to act as the core fusion-inhibitory element by altering membrane biophysical properties18. However, these “snapshot” studies leave two fundamental challenges unresolved. First, while the precise membrane topology of IFITM3 has been historically debated (with models proposing Type I, Type II, or intramembrane orientations)15,19,20, recent evidence lar- gely supports a Type II topology7,17,19,21,22. Although specific sequence motifs are known to influence its activity, the field still lacks a high-resolution functionalmapanchoredtothisphysicalstructure18,23–25.Second,theclinical interpretation of IFITM3 variation is lagging. Of the ~270 rare missense variants identified in humans, fewer than 20 are functionally classified, leaving most variants classified as of uncertain significance (VUS)26–28. Computational predictors are increasingly used to prioritize candidate pathogenic variants. However, their performance on antiviral restriction factors, particularly membrane-associated proteins such as IFITM3, remains largely untested against comprehensive experimental datasets29–32. Resolving these questions requires measurements at a scale impossible to achieve through conventional one-by-one mutagenesis. Deep mutational scanning (DMS) provides a powerful framework for experimentally mea- suring the functional consequences of protein variation in a high- throughput manner33–43. However, many prior DMS studies relied on sampling-based mutagenesis strategies or incomplete variant libraries. A fully synthesized, position-complete, and unbiased saturation landscape that captures all possible amino acid substitutions across an entire protein 1State Key Laboratory for Diagnosis and Treatment of Infectious Diseases, National Clinical Research Center for Infectious Diseases, Collaborative Innovation Center for Diagnosis and Treatment of Infectious Diseases, The First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China. 2Department of Laboratory Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China. e-mail: jianchen76@zju.edu.cn; minzheng@zju.edu.cn Communications Biology Article in Press 1234567890():,; 1234567890():,; has remained rare, particularly in the context of functional mapping of antiviral activity. Here, we employed deep mutational scanning (DMS) to generated a position-complete saturation mutagenesis library encompassing 2898 IFITM3 variants. We quantified variant fitness against three influenza A viruses, including the avian-origin H7N9 strain and two H1N1 laboratory strains (PR8 and WSN) that differ in entry and fusion requirements44. By testing these distinct viral entry pathways within a unified screening fra- mework, we: (1) reveal a mutational constraint pattern most consistent with experimentally supported Type II topology framework; (2) identify key biophysical features underlying the antiviral activity of the intramembrane domain; (3) benchmark the performance and limitations of current pathogenicity prediction models; and (4) provide an experimental frame- work for the interpretation and prioritization of IFITM3 variants identified in human populations. Results DMS of IFITM3 across multiple IAV strains and cellular contexts To map the functional determinants of IFITM3-mediated viral restriction, we executed a deep mutational scanning (DMS) screen encompassing all 133 residues under the selective pressure of influenza A virus (IAV) (Fig. 1A). We constructed two independent pooled lentiviral saturation mutagenesis libraries, comprising 2508 missense, 126 synonymous (SYN), 132 nonsense (STOP), and 132 deletion (DEL) variants. Next-generation sequencing verified plasmid library quality, showing >99% coverage of the intended variants and a uniform abundance distribution (log10 variance <0.5) (Fig. 1B, C). Following stable transduction into interferon-deficient HEK293T cells45–48 and IFITM3-null A549 cells (IFITM3-KO clone2, Supplementary Fig. 1A, B), expression of the variant libraries did not significantly affect baseline cell viability (Supplementary Fig. 1C), and library representation remained highly uniform in both cell types (Supplementary Fig. 1D). Validation assays confirmed that library-expressing cells retained antiviral activity against all three viruses (Supplementary Fig. 1E). To assess the antiviral function of each mutation, the library-expressing cells were sub- sequently challenged with three antigenically distinct influenza A virus (IAV) strains: the laboratory-adapted H1N1 strains PR8 and WSN, and a clinical avian-origin H7N9 isolate. Infected (NP + ) and uninfected (NP-) cells were isolated via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) (Supple- mentary Fig. 1F) to quantify variant abundance shifts. We found that antiviral fitness scores derived from deep sequencing were highly repro- ducible between biological replicates (Spearman’s ρ > 0.5) (Fig. 1D–G). As expected, nonsense variants abolished antiviral activity, synonymous var- iants clustered near wild-type levels, whereas missense and deletion variants spanned a broad range of fitness scores(Fig. 1H–M). This approach enables systematic dissection of host–virus interactions at single-amino-acid resolution. The functional landscape reveals domain-specific mutational constraints To assess whether mutational effects were conserved across the influenza A virus strains examined here, variant-level fitness scores from the primary A549 dataset were visualized as mutational landscapes (Fig. 2A–C), with corresponding HEK293T datasets shown in Supplementary Fig. 2A–C. High correlations between viral datasets indicate that mutational effects on IFITM3 function are broadly conserved across the influenza A virus strains examined in this study (Supplementary Fig. 3A–F). To evaluate domain- specific sensitivity, missense variants within each structural domain were benchmarked against internal synonymous controls from the correspond- ing domain19,20 (Fig. 2D–F, Supplementary Fig. 2D–F). The N-terminal region (residues 2–55) and distal C-terminal tail (residues 131–133) exhibited comparatively lower mutational constraint than the membrane- associated core of IFITM3. However, this tolerance was not uniform, with specific functional elements remaining strongly constrained. Notably, substitutions within the conserved endocytic YXXΦ trafficking motif (residues20–23)markedlycompromisedantiviralactivity49.Conversely,the central membrane-associated core (residues 59–130), comprising the amphipathic helix (AH), conserved intracellular loop (CIL), and trans- membrane domain (TMD), displayed substantially reduced mutational tolerance. Although traditional hydropathy-based algorithms identify only residues ~59–68 as a membrane-inserted segment18, our DMS data indicate that the downstream helices (CIL and TMD) are similarly constrained, consistent with a more extended membrane-associated architecture than predicted by hydropathy-based models alone. Evolutionary conservation and DMS identify a structurally con- strained functional core within IFITM3 To examine the extent to which evolutionary conservation captures mutational tolerance, we compiled IFITM3 orthologs from 33 representa- tive vertebrate species spanning major evolutionary lineages, generated a multiple-sequence alignment (Supplementary Fig. 4, Supplementary Fig. 5A), and compared site-wise conservation scores with DMS-derived fitness measurements across IFITM3 (Fig. 3A, B). Positions exhibiting high evolutionary conservation generally displayed reduced mutational toler- ance,resultinginsignificantcorrelationsbetweenconservationandantiviral fitness across all three viral datasets (Spearman’s R = –0.67 to –0.72, P < 0.001; Fig. 3C–E), with similar relationships observed in HEK293T cells (Supplementary Fig. 5B–E). These results indicate that evolutionary con- servation is broadly associated with functional importance across IFITM3. Consistent with this relationship, several previously characterized reg- ulatory residues were among the most constrained positions in our dataset, including the palmitoylated cysteines C71, C72, and C10516, as well as ubiquitination-associated lysines K83, K84, and K10450 (Supplementary Fig. 5F). The concordance between evolutionary conservation, prior mechanistic studies, and DMS-derived fitness measurements further sup- ports the biological validity of the functional landscape generated in this study. Having established a global relationship between evolutionary con- servation and antiviral fitness, we next asked whether mutational con- straints clustered within specific regions of the IFITM3 structure. We mapped DMS fitness scores onto the experimentally validated Type II membrane topology and found that functional constraintsare concentrated within the central CD225 domain, which encompasses the majority of residues exhibiting strong intolerance to mutation (Fig. 4A). Notably, this region contains a recently proposed 53-residue R-SNARE-like motif 51. Several residues implicated in this motif, including F75, F78, R85, and G95, were highly sensitive to amino acid substitution and consistently displayed severe losses of antiviral activity (Fig. 3B). Among these, R85 corresponds to the central “0” layer residue proposed within the SNARE-like architecture and emerged as one of the most mutation-intolerant positions across the entireprotein.TheclosecorrespondencebetweentheproposedSNARE-like motifandthemutationallyconstrainedcoreidentifiedbyDMSsuggeststhat preservation of this region is a major determinant of IFITM3 antiviral activity and may reflect structural or functional requirements associated with SNARE-like interactions51. Todefinethestructuralbasisoftheseconstraints,weanalyzedthethree membrane-associated helical segments individually (designated Helices 1–3) (Fig. 4A, Supplementary Fig. 6A). Within Helix 1 (the amphipathic helix, AH), antiviral efficacy correlated strictly with amphipathic geometry52,53. To quantify this relationship, we evaluated mutation-induced alterationsinthehydrophobic moment(〈μH〉) across218single-aminoacid substitutions54 (Fig. 4B), and calculated mutation-induced changes in the hydrophobic moment (Fig. 4C). Disrupting the hydrophobic anchors (e.g., F63, L66) significantly compromised function, while introducing hydro- phobic residues onto the polar face (e.g., L62, M68) similarly abolished restriction18. Distinct outliers, such as W60 and N64, implied additional requirements beyond pure amphipathicity, likely involving interfacial aro- matic packing or specific lipid headgroup interactions23–25(Fig. 4C). Helix 2 (residues 70–88) displayed uniformly strong mutational intolerance (Fig. 4D). Unlike the amphipathic Helix 1, this segment exhibited high https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-026-10800-0 Article Communications Biology Article in Press average hydrophobicity (〈H〉= 1.133) and a low hydrophobic moment (〈μH〉= 0.179) (Fig. 4E), consistent with a deeply membrane-embedded region extending into a structurally constrained cytosolic loop (residues 81–88) (Supplementary Fig. 6B). Particularly strong fitness defects were observed upon mutation of residues surrounding Y80 and K83, suggesting the notion that the integrity of this intramembrane region is critical for antiviral function24,55. Within Helix 3 (residues 92–130), mutational intol- erance exhibited a pronounced helical periodicity. Mapping fitness scores onto the helical wheel revealed a clear segregation of constrained and tol- erant residues onto opposite faces of the helix (Fig. 4F, G). Highly con- strained residues, including D92, G95, and K104, clustered on one face, whereas neighboring residues on the opposing face, such as V93, T94, and https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-026-10800-0 Article Communications Biology Article in Press Q97, remained comparatively tolerant to substitution. This asymmetric distribution identifies a putative functional surface within Helix 3 and suggeststhatantiviralactivitydependsoninteractionsmediatedbyaspecific helical interface rather than the transmembrane segment as a whole53,56. Collectively, these analyses demonstrate that mutational constraints are highly structured across IFITM3 rather than uniformly distributed. Distinct classes of functional requirements emerge within different membrane- associated helices, including maintenance of amphipathic architecture in Helix 1, structural integrity of the intramembrane region in Helix 2, and a face-specific constraint pattern within Helix 3. Together, these features define the major determinants underlying IFITM3-mediated antiviral activity17,19,20,22. Experimental functional maps expose systematic limitations in AI-based pathogenicity predictors Toevaluatetherelationshipbetweenexperimentallymeasuredfitnessscores and computational variant effect prediction, we benchmarked our DMS- derived fitness scores against AlphaMissense pathogenicity predictions, which estimate the likelihood that a missense variant disrupts protein function based on evolutionary and structural information29. Across all variants, AlphaMissense scores showed a significant overall correlation with antiviral fitness, with variants classified as “likely pathogenic” generally exhibiting reduced IFITM3-mediated restriction (Fig. 5A, B). However, several classes of variants deviated substantially from this trend. In parti- cular, AlphaMissense showed limited sensitivity to functionally important residues within the disordered N- and C-terminal regions and, by design, could not identify variants with enhanced antiviral activity, highlighting the complementary value of experimental measurements. To facilitate directcomparison, we categorized DMS fitness scores into loss of antiviral activity, WT-like (tolerant), and enhanced antiviral activity classes using empirical thresholds anchored to the distributions of synon- ymous and nonsense variants (Supplementary Fig. 7A, 7B). This analysis revealed three major classes of discordance between computational and experimental assessments: (i) “benign-but-intolerant” variants, enriched within N- and C-terminal regulatory regions; (ii) “pathogenic-but-tolerant” variants, concentrated within the intramembrane domain (residues 88–110); and (iii) variants assigned ambiguous pathogenicity scores that could be functionally resolved by DMS measurements (Fig. 5C). These discordant variants were unevenly distributed across the IFITM3 sequence (Supplementary Fig. 7C, D). Notably, predictions were largely concordant within the amphipathic helix (residues 68–80), whereas variants associated with lipid-dependent interactions or topology-related constraints were more frequently misclassified. To independently evaluate discordant variants, we selected repre- sentative substitutions for individual validation (Fig. 5D, E). Immunoblot analysis demonstrated that most variants accumulated to levels comparable to wild-type IFITM3 (Fig. 5F). analysis.summary_en: This study presents a high-resolution functional map of 2,898 IFITM3 variants across three influenza A strains, revealing a functionally constrained central region that aligns with a Type II membrane topology. The research highlights structural features linked to antiviral activity and identifies limitations in computational models in predicting the effects of variants in unstructured regions. The findings offer a functional readout for rare human alleles that may affect susceptibility to influenza infection, providing a resource for understanding human variation and a framework for studying host-directed antiviral mechanisms. The study contributes to the understanding of how genetic differences in IFITM3 influence influenza outcomes, but it does not address the broader implications for public health or treatment strategies.

title_zh: IFITM3功能图谱解析其抗病毒药物核心并阐明人类流感易感性
source_body_en: Genetic variation in interferon-induced transmembrane protein 3 (IFITM3) contributes to inter-individual differences in influenza outcome, yet a comprehensive functional map of IFITM3 variation remains unavailable. Here we show a high-resolution functional atlas of 2,898 IFITM3 variants across three influenza A strains using deep mutational scanning. Our data reveals a functionally constrained central region, providing functional evidence consistent with a Type II membrane topology and highlighting structural features associated with antiviral activity. Comparison with AlphaMissense reveals systematic limitations in predicting the effects of variants within unstructured N-terminal motifs and lipid-embedded domains. Crucially, computational models fail to recognize variants with enhanced antiviral activity, such as G133Q. By integrating this atlas with ClinVar and gnomAD, we provide a functional readout for rare human alleles that may influence susceptibility to infection. These findings provide a resource for interpreting human variation and establish a framework for studying host-directed antiviral mechanisms. This study generates a high-resolution functional atlas of 2,898 IFITM3 variants using deep mutational scanning. The resulting map resolves the protein’s intramembrane antiviral core and identifies key rare human alleles that dictate susceptibility to influenza infection

title: Non-coding RNAs and RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway: Insights for targeted therapy in influenza infection

source_records.title: Non-coding RNAs and RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway: Insights for targeted therapy in influenza infection
Non-coding RNAs and RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway: Insights for targeted therapy in influenza infection

priority_tier_reason: 高相关性，且具备高等级研究设计、全文证据或较强数据库/引用支持
full_text: Influenza viruses are a significant challenge to the health of the global population, and are responsible for millions of severe cases and hundreds of thousands of deaths each year. The outbreaks of pandemics can result from the rapid antigenic drift and shift of the virus, which can also affect the effectiveness of the existing vaccines. Despite the availability of antiviral drugs like neuraminidase inhibitors, the rise in resistant strains is indicative of the urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies with distinct mechanisms of action. Developing treatment approaches that target host-directed pathways essential for viral replication and the immune response could be a pivotal step in mitigating this issue. The key pathway central to this strategy is the innate immune-sensing pathway mediated by retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and its adaptor protein mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS).[] This axis serves as the first line of intracellular defense, recognizing viral RNA (vRNA) and triggering a potent antiviral state through the induction of type I interferons (IFN-I) and hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). The fundamental function of the RIG-I/MAVS pathway in regulating influenza A and B virus replication in the respiratory epithelium is well-established.[] However, the activation of this pathway is complex and not merely a simple on/off switch. To play its role in eradicating the virus without causing excessive inflammation and immunopathology, it must be succinctly and tightly regulated. Notably, a diverse array of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs), has been identified as key regulators of this delicate balance.[] This editorial highlights the complex regulatory networks orchestrated by ncRNAs on the RIG-I/MAVS signaling hub during influenza infection and discusses their translational potential as targets for next-generation, host-directed antiviral therapies. The RIG-I/MAVS Pathway: A Central Hub and Antiviral Battleground During infection, the vRNA of the influenza virus is recognized by the RIG-I receptor of the host cell. The RIG-I binds to the viral double-stranded RNA via its C-terminal helicase domain, thus triggering a conformational change that exposes its N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD). Subsequently, the E3 ubiquitin ligase tripartite motif containing 25 (TRIM25) mediates K63-linked ubiquitination of the CARD domains. The ubiquitinated RIG-I activates the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS using its CARD domain, thus triggering a cascade that mobilizes interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) to produce IFN-I and cytokines, mounting a crucial antiviral defense. In addition, the RIG-I/MAVS pathway participates in antiviral innate immunity, as well as influences the host’s acquired immunological response. RIG-I signaling through MAVS is vital for generating strong, multi-functional T-cell responses to influenza A viruses (IAVs), which helps control initial infection, promotes immune memory, and provides broad protection against different IAV strains.[] The significance of this pathway is highlighted by the presence of evolved advanced mechanisms that influenza viruses have developed to directly inhibit RIG-I and TRIM25, particularly through their non-structural protein 1 (NS1), which significantly reduces the host’s IFN response.[] The host defense continuously counters viral infection, and the RIG-I/MAVS axis is the core pathway facilitating this. Furthermore, the host utilizes complex feedback systems to regulate this pathway and modulate host antiviral response, and ncRNAs play an important role during this process.[] Diverse ncRNAs as Fine-Tuners of the Antiviral Immune Response ncRNAs regulate the RIG-I/MAVS axis at multiple levels to ensure a balanced antiviral immune response while mitigating immune-mediated pathology. Their actions can be broadly categorized into proviral (suppressing immunity) or antiviral (enhancing immunity), though some exhibit context-dependent functions.[] miRNAs: Precision tools for immune modulation These small (~22 nt) RNAs primarily function by binding to complementary sequences in the 3’ untranslated region (UTR) of target messenger RNA (mRNAs), leading to transcript degradation or translational repression. The influenza virus exploits host miRNA expression to undermine antiviral immunity. This is achieved through specific mechanisms, such as miR-218 directly targeting the 3′UTR of RIG-I (DExD/H-box helicase 58, DDX58) mRNA, and miR-202-5p inhibiting the expression of TRIM25, both of which are critical components of the RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway.[] By disrupting these processes, the virus effectively reduces the activation of the signaling cascade and facilitates immune evasion [Supplementary Figure 1, http://links.lww.com/CM9/D6]. Similarly, miR-122 and miR-125a/b are upregulated during infection and target MAVS mRNA, attenuating the downstream antiviral signal.[] In contrast, the host can use miRNAs to strengthen its defense. For instance, miR-136 can function as an endogenous ligand for RIG-I, directly increasing its activation.[] In addition, miR-483-3p is transported via exosomes from infected cells and functions as a signaling molecule to activate the innate immune response in nearby cells.[] Moreover, miR-200c improves the stability of MAVS protein by reducing the activity of its negative regulators, contactin 1 (CNTN1) and ubiquitin specific peptidase 25 (USP25), demonstrating a method to strengthen the central signaling node. Collectively, these findings reveal a bidirectional link between the influenza virus and host miRNAs. The virus utilizes miRNAs to inhibit RIG-I/MAVS signaling as a means of evading the immune response, whereas the host employs other miRNAs to strengthen antiviral defenses via direct receptor activation, paracrine priming, or the stabilization of essential signaling components. lncRNAs: Complex regulators with multifaceted roles These are longer RNA transcripts (>200 nt) that regulate gene expression through diverse mechanisms, including acting as decoys, scaffolds, or guides. Their participation in the RIG-I/MAVS pathway introduces an additional layer of complexity. For instance, during viral infection, the lncRNA antivirus and activate neutrophil (AVAN) is induced, and this promotes the TRIM25-mediated ubiquitination of RIG-I by serving as a molecular scaffold, thereby enhancing IFN production [Supplementary Figure 1, http://links.lww.com/CM9/D6].[] Another regulatory mechanism is exemplified by MAVS antiviral-related lncRNA (MARL), which acts as a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) or “sponge” for miR-122. By sequestering miR-122, MARL prevents it from degrading MAVS mRNA, thereby up-regulating MAVS protein levels and promoting the antiviral state. In contrast, lnc-Lsm3b plays a crucial role as a feedback inhibitor in the late stages of infection. It has a stronger affinity for RIG-I than vRNA, keeping it in an inactive conformation and preventing sustained IFN production, which shields the host against severe inflammation.[] Thus, lncRNAs dynamically balance antiviral defense and immune homeostasis by both activating and suppressing the RIG-I/MAVS pathway at different stages of infection. circRNAs: Stable mediators with direct and indirect functions These covalently closed, non-polyadenylated RNAs are highly stable and can function as miRNA sponges, protein decoys, or even templates for translation. Their involvement in antiviral immunity is a promising and rapidly evolving field of study. Some unmodified circRNAs can be directly recognized by RIG-I, leading to the activation of the innate immune response. Particularly, it has been demonstrated that circular RNA vesicle-associated membrane protein 3 (circVAMP3) directly binds to and sequesters the viral nucleoprotein (NP) and non-structural protein 1 (NS1) proteins to prevent influenza virus replication [Supplementary Figure 1, http://links.lww.com/CM9/D6]. This sequestration impairs the activity of the viral ribonucleoprotein complex and, as a secondary effect, relieves RIG-I from NS1-mediated inhibition, thereby restoring IFN signaling.[] In addition, circular phosphoinositide kinase FYVE-type zinc finger containing RNA (circPIKfyve) enhances the MAVS-mediated antiviral response by sponging miR-21-3p, a miRNA that normally suppresses MAVS expression. By neutralizing miR-21-3p, circPIKfyve upregulates MAVS levels, thereby strengthening the host’s ability to combat viral infection. Targeting ncRNAs for Therapeutic Intervention: Strategies, Challenges, and Prospects The intricate interplay between the influenza virus, host ncRNAs, and the RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway presents a novel target for antiviral therapy. ncRNAs can precisely regulate key stages of the antiviral immune response. They can, however, either promote RIG-I/MAVS signaling to increase IFN production or decrease it to aid in viral immune evasion. Consequently, the potential therapeutic strategy (summarized in the Supplementary Table 1, http://links.lww.com/CM9/D6) involves using RNA-based drugs (such as mimics or inhibitors) to modulate specific ncRNAs. This will enhance beneficial immune responses while simultaneously suppressing excessive and detrimental inflammation. Nevertheless, implementing this strategy in practice encounters two primary challenges. The first challenge is related to delivery. RNA therapeutics require carriers to achieve targeted delivery, cellular uptake, and endosomal escape. Current mainstream carriers like lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) exhibit liver tropism, making repeated pulmonary dosing difficult. Alternative carriers such as exosomes and polymeric nanoparticles offer greater targeting potential but face their own challenges, including production scalability, drug loading efficiency, and batch-to-batch consistency. The second challenge is specificity and safety. Hepatotoxicity, which is primarily a side effect of non-specific binding of RNA interference (RNAi) sequences rather than chemical toxicity, is a key off-target effect of RNAi therapeutics. This puts a great deal of pressure on the development of the precise design of guide RNAs. In the future, multidisciplinary and collaborative innovation is needed to advance ncRNA-based treatments, with the primary goal of developing next-generation, lung-optimized delivery systems. For instance, modifying the surface proteins of exosomes may improve their ability to target the lungs, although issues concerning scalable manufacturing need to be addressed. Furthermore, it is important to incorporate systems biology and artificial intelligence (AI). Utilizing multi-omics data to map ncRNA regulatory networks and employing AI models to accurately predict and circumvent off-target risks will enable the rational design of these therapeutics. Furthermore, determining the optimal therapeutic “window” is crucial. Future research should identify dynamic biomarkers and utilize AI analysis to predict individual patient immune response trajectories, which can then facilitate the development of personalized treatment regimens. Ultimately, clinical translation will likely depend on combination strategies, such as pairing ncRNA-targeting agents with direct-acting antivirals or immunomodulators. Progress in this field also necessitates the development of more predictive preclinical models that better replicate human lung physiology and immune responses. In conclusion, by converging advances in nanotechnology, bioinformatics, and immunology, targeting ncRNAs holds the promise of pioneering a new class of precision medicines against influenza and other respiratory viral infections. full_text_sections.full_text: Influenza viruses are a significant challenge to the health of the global population, and are responsible for millions of severe cases and hundreds of thousands of deaths each year. The outbreaks of pandemics can result from the rapid antigenic drift and shift of the virus, which can also affect the effectiveness of the existing vaccines. Despite the availability of antiviral drugs like neuraminidase inhibitors, the rise in resistant strains is indicative of the urgent need for novel therapeutic strategies with distinct mechanisms of action. Developing treatment approaches that target host-directed pathways essential for viral replication and the immune response could be a pivotal step in mitigating this issue. The key pathway central to this strategy is the innate immune-sensing pathway mediated by retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and its adaptor protein mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein (MAVS).[] This axis serves as the first line of intracellular defense, recognizing viral RNA (vRNA) and triggering a potent antiviral state through the induction of type I interferons (IFN-I) and hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs). The fundamental function of the RIG-I/MAVS pathway in regulating influenza A and B virus replication in the respiratory epithelium is well-established.[] However, the activation of this pathway is complex and not merely a simple on/off switch. To play its role in eradicating the virus without causing excessive inflammation and immunopathology, it must be succinctly and tightly regulated. Notably, a diverse array of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs), including microRNAs (miRNAs), long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), and circular RNAs (circRNAs), has been identified as key regulators of this delicate balance.[] This editorial highlights the complex regulatory networks orchestrated by ncRNAs on the RIG-I/MAVS signaling hub during influenza infection and discusses their translational potential as targets for next-generation, host-directed antiviral therapies. The RIG-I/MAVS Pathway: A Central Hub and Antiviral Battleground During infection, the vRNA of the influenza virus is recognized by the RIG-I receptor of the host cell. The RIG-I binds to the viral double-stranded RNA via its C-terminal helicase domain, thus triggering a conformational change that exposes its N-terminal caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD). Subsequently, the E3 ubiquitin ligase tripartite motif containing 25 (TRIM25) mediates K63-linked ubiquitination of the CARD domains. The ubiquitinated RIG-I activates the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS using its CARD domain, thus triggering a cascade that mobilizes interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF3) and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells (NF-κB) to produce IFN-I and cytokines, mounting a crucial antiviral defense. In addition, the RIG-I/MAVS pathway participates in antiviral innate immunity, as well as influences the host’s acquired immunological response. RIG-I signaling through MAVS is vital for generating strong, multi-functional T-cell responses to influenza A viruses (IAVs), which helps control initial infection, promotes immune memory, and provides broad protection against different IAV strains.[] The significance of this pathway is highlighted by the presence of evolved advanced mechanisms that influenza viruses have developed to directly inhibit RIG-I and TRIM25, particularly through their non-structural protein 1 (NS1), which significantly reduces the host’s IFN response.[] The host defense continuously counters viral infection, and the RIG-I/MAVS axis is the core pathway facilitating this. Furthermore, the host utilizes complex feedback systems to regulate this pathway and modulate host antiviral response, and ncRNAs play an important role during this process.[] Diverse ncRNAs as Fine-Tuners of the Antiviral Immune Response ncRNAs regulate the RIG-I/MAVS axis at multiple levels to ensure a balanced antiviral immune response while mitigating immune-mediated pathology. Their actions can be broadly categorized into proviral (suppressing immunity) or antiviral (enhancing immunity), though some exhibit context-dependent functions.[] miRNAs: Precision tools for immune modulation These small (~22 nt) RNAs primarily function by binding to complementary sequences in the 3’ untranslated region (UTR) of target messenger RNA (mRNAs), leading to transcript degradation or translational repression. The influenza virus exploits host miRNA expression to undermine antiviral immunity. This is achieved through specific mechanisms, such as miR-218 directly targeting the 3′UTR of RIG-I (DExD/H-box helicase 58, DDX58) mRNA, and miR-202-5p inhibiting the expression of TRIM25, both of which are critical components of the RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway.[] By disrupting these processes, the virus effectively reduces the activation of the signaling cascade and facilitates immune evasion [Supplementary Figure 1, http://links.lww.com/CM9/D6]. Similarly, miR-122 and miR-125a/b are upregulated during infection and target MAVS mRNA, attenuating the downstream antiviral signal.[] In contrast, the host can use miRNAs to strengthen its defense. For instance, miR-136 can function as an endogenous ligand for RIG-I, directly increasing its activation.[] In addition, miR-483-3p is transported via exosomes from infected cells and functions as a signaling molecule to activate the innate immune response in nearby cells.[] Moreover, miR-200c improves the stability of MAVS protein by reducing the activity of its negative regulators, contactin 1 (CNTN1) and ubiquitin specific peptidase 25 (USP25), demonstrating a method to strengthen the central signaling node. Collectively, these findings reveal a bidirectional link between the influenza virus and host miRNAs. The virus utilizes miRNAs to inhibit RIG-I/MAVS signaling as a means of evading the immune response, whereas the host employs other miRNAs to strengthen antiviral defenses via direct receptor activation, paracrine priming, or the stabilization of essential signaling components. lncRNAs: Complex regulators with multifaceted roles These are longer RNA transcripts (>200 nt) that regulate gene expression through diverse mechanisms, including acting as decoys, scaffolds, or guides. Their participation in the RIG-I/MAVS pathway introduces an additional layer of complexity. For instance, during viral infection, the lncRNA antivirus and activate neutrophil (AVAN) is induced, and this promotes the TRIM25-mediated ubiquitination of RIG-I by serving as a molecular scaffold, thereby enhancing IFN production [Supplementary Figure 1, http://links.lww.com/CM9/D6].[] Another regulatory mechanism is exemplified by MAVS antiviral-related lncRNA (MARL), which acts as a competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) or “sponge” for miR-122. By sequestering miR-122, MARL prevents it from degrading MAVS mRNA, thereby up-regulating MAVS protein levels and promoting the antiviral state. In contrast, lnc-Lsm3b plays a crucial role as a feedback inhibitor in the late stages of infection. It has a stronger affinity for RIG-I than vRNA, keeping it in an inactive conformation and preventing sustained IFN production, which shields the host against severe inflammation.[] Thus, lncRNAs dynamically balance antiviral defense and immune homeostasis by both activating and suppressing the RIG-I/MAVS pathway at different stages of infection. circRNAs: Stable mediators with direct and indirect functions These covalently closed, non-polyadenylated RNAs are highly stable and can function as miRNA sponges, protein decoys, or even templates for translation. Their involvement in antiviral immunity is a promising and rapidly evolving field of study. Some unmodified circRNAs can be directly recognized by RIG-I, leading to the activation of the innate immune response. Particularly, it has been demonstrated that circular RNA vesicle-associated membrane protein 3 (circVAMP3) directly binds to and sequesters the viral nucle…

title_original: Non-coding RNAs and RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway: Insights for targeted therapy in influenza infection

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study investigates the role of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) in modulating the RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway during influenza infection, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies due to the limitations of current antiviral drugs.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focuses on the RIG-I/MAVS pathway and its interaction with ncRNAs in the context of influenza infection, with an emphasis on the innate and adaptive immune responses in human respiratory epithelium.
analysis.methods: The research employs molecular and cellular techniques to explore how ncRNAs, including miRNAs, lncRNAs, and circRNAs, regulate the RIG-I/MAVS pathway, with specific attention to the binding and sequestration of viral proteins by circVAMP3.
analysis.main_results: It was demonstrated that circVAMP3 directly binds to and sequesters the viral nucleoprotein (NP) and non-structural protein 1 (NS1) to prevent influenza virus replication, as shown in Supplementary Figure 1.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study interprets the findings as evidence of a bidirectional interaction between the influenza virus and host miRNAs, suggesting that ncRNAs could serve as novel therapeutic targets for antiviral intervention.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings offer insights into the development of host-directed antiviral therapies that could potentially mitigate the impact of influenza by targeting ncRNAs involved in immune regulation.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on molecular mechanisms without direct clinical outcomes, and the evidence is based on in vitro and in silico analyses, which may not fully reflect in vivo conditions.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the role of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) in modulating the RIG-I/MAVS signaling pathway during influenza infection. It highlights the limitations of current antiviral drugs due to the emergence of resistant strains and emphasizes the need for novel therapeutic strategies. The research identifies ncRNAs, including miRNAs, lncRNAs, and circRNAs, as key regulators of the immune response, with a specific focus on circVAMP3, which sequesters viral proteins to inhibit replication. The findings suggest a bidirectional interaction between the virus and host miRNAs, offering potential for host-directed antiviral therapies. However, the study is limited to in vitro and in silico analyses, which may not fully capture in vivo complexities. The results have implications for the development of precision medicines targeting ncRNAs to combat influenza and other respiratory viral infections.

title: A bivalent inactivated influenza vaccine incorporating epitope-optimized surface proteins confers cross-protective immunity against H9N2 influenza virus
abstract: The H9N2 avian influenza virus (AIV) has caused substantial economic losses to the global poultry industry and poses a zoonotic threat to humans. Vaccination constitutes a pivotal strategy for the prevention and control of H9N2 AIVs. However, the ongoing antigenic evolution of the viruses pose a persistent challenge to the protective efficacy of existing vaccines. Therefore, the development of a broadly protective H9N2 influenza vaccine capable of eliciting cross-reactive immune responses is crucial for mitigating both the disease burden and the risk of pandemics. Here, we developed a bivalent chimeric inactivated vaccine, designated cHANA, by combining two individually rescued chimeric inactivated viruses, cHANA1 and cHANA2. Each recombinant virus carries one set of Epigraph-designed HA and NA immunogens, and the two sets were computationally optimized from global H9N2 HA and NA sequence datasets to complement each other in epitope coverage across the H9N2 viral population. Compared to the WHO-recommended candidate vaccine virus (CVV), AL/39, cHANA elicited more potent cross-reactive antibody responses and T cell immunity in mice. Furthermore, it elicited effective cross-protection against lethal challenge with heterologous H9N2 virus and significantly reduced pulmonary viral loads of mice. By conferring broad protective immunity, this vaccine represents a promising universal vaccine candidate for controlling H9N2 outbreaks.

title: Baculovirus-based production of virus-like particles for avian influenza: development, immunogenicity, and cross-protection against H5 and H7 AIVs
abstract: The persistent threat of H5 and H7 highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) necessitates effective broad-spectrum vaccines. This study systematically evaluated the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of H5N6 virus-like particle (H5N6-VLP) vaccine and subsequently developed a trivalent VLP vaccine (H5N6-H5N8-H7N9-VLP) using the baculovirus expression system (BEVS). Production of H5N6-VLP was optimized at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1 to achieve efficient assembly. The H5N6-VLP vaccine induced potent immune responses in specific-pathogen-free (SPF) chickens, providing 100% protection against homologous H5N6-GD154 virus when the HA titer reached 9 log2. Compared with traditional inactivated vaccines, the H5N6-VLP vaccine induced faster humoral immune responses and higher CD8+ T cell proportions. The HI seroconversion rate was 30% on day 7 post-immunization (0% for inactivated vaccine), reached 100% by day 10, while it was only 80% on day 14 for the inactivated vaccine. Furthermore, the protective efficacy of the H5N6-VLP vaccine was associated with increased IFN‐γ expression and elevated proportions of B cells and CD8+ T cells. Although both vaccines provided complete homologous protection, the H5N6-VLP vaccine showed better cross-protection against the heterologous H5N1-D889 strain (70% vs. 40%). A delayed challenge experiment further demonstrated that the H5N6-VLP vaccine induced durable immunity, with HI titers remaining above the protective threshold and 100% protection against homologous challenge at 8 weeks post-immunization. Based on these findings, a trivalent H5N6-H5N8-H7N9-VLP vaccine was developed. The trivalent vaccine induced substantial antibody responses and provided complete protection against parental and circulating strains, with efficacy comparable to a commercial inactivated vaccine and no detectable antigenic interference between components. Our findings highlight the potential of the BEVS-derived H5N6-VLP vaccine, particularly its early antibody induction, which allows rapid flock protection during acute HPAI outbreaks, and its cross-reactivity against heterologous strains. Furthermore, the trivalent vaccine formulation extends the potential application of this VLP platform for broad-spectrum HPAI control.

title: Newton Divided Difference Optimization for Fingerprint-Based Neural Virtual Screening against Avian Influenza A/H9N2
abstract: Avian influenza A/H9N2 poses persistent zoonotic and veterinary threats, yet efficient computational tools for antiviral compound prioritization remain underdeveloped, particularly with respect to optimizer behavior in high-dimensional neural screening. This study proposes Newton Divided Difference (NDD) optimization, a lightweight positive diagonal curvature-aware training strategy, as a novel optimizer for fingerprint-based neural virtual screening against avian influenza A/H9N2, with the objective of evaluating its performance across aligned molecular fingerprint representations and chemically structured validation protocols. An aligned benchmark of 1,459 molecules consisting of 615 candidate active compounds and 844 decoys was represented by EState (79 features), PubChem (881 features), and Klekota–Roth (4,860 features) fingerprints, sharing identical molecule identities, labels, and split assignments. A fixed multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifier was trained with NDD and seven baseline optimizers under stratified, scaffold-key, and similarity-cluster split protocols across five repeated seeds. NDD achieved the highest descriptive ROC-AUC (Receiver Operating Characteriztic – Area Under the Curve) and PR-AUC (Precision-Recall Area Under the Curve) on Klekota–Roth fingerprints under scaffold-key and similarity-cluster protocols, and remained competitive under the stratified split with ROC-AUC of 0.9872. Architecture-sensitivity tests confirmed stable NDD performance across multiple network configurations, with ROC-AUC values ranging from 0.9876 to 0.9890. Compared with Hessian-free optimization, NDD reduced per-run runtime from approximately 50–54 seconds to approximately 8 seconds on Klekota–Roth under the same CPU-only configuration while achieving comparable ranking performance. The novelty of this work lies in the first systematic assessment of NDD for H9N2 neural virtual screening, demonstrating that positive diagonal curvature-aware scaling provides a practical, stable, and computationally efficient optimization alternative in sparse high-dimensional ligand-based screening settings, although external validation and prospective experimental confirmation remain necessary before practical antiviral prioritization.
